entries.text: Hi, it’s Claudio Baccigalupo. This week’s changes to the Rails codebase have a strong focus on security, from a rewritten guide to safer defaults for new apps. Rewrite the Securing Rails guide As part of the Rails Foundation documentation effort, the refreshed guide drops outdated sections and old gems, adds a new section on cookies, and covers file uploads with Active Storage. Patch Rack::Multipart::Parser to not allow arbitrary encoding Multipart form data submitted in arbitrary encodings has little to no legitimate use, but it has been used several times in exploit chains targeting Rails applications. Rails now patches Rack to disregard it. The change is also backported to 8.1 and 8.0. If your app depends on that behavior, opt out with: config.action_dispatch.allow_rack_multipart_encoding = true Harden generated GitHub Actions workflows The ci.yml of new apps pins the versions of actions to a SHA to mitigate repointed git tag attacks, in a format that Dependabot keeps up to date. ruby/setup-ruby stays unpinned so new Ruby releases are available right away. Checkout actions also set persist-credentials: false, so later steps can’t read GitHub tokens from the filesystem. Add config.active_record.association_scope_keeps_owner_conditions unscope(where: ...), unscope(:where) and rewhere in an association scope could remove the condition that ties the records to their owner, so update_all, delete_all and dependent: :delete_all could affect records of other owners. entries.summary: Marco Roth, independent consultant and the creator of Herb and ReActionView, joins Robby to talk about teaching Rails to understand its own templates.
entries.text: Marco Roth, independent consultant and the creator of Herb and ReActionView, joins Robby to talk about teaching Rails to understand its own templates. Marco explains how Herb parses HTML and ERB together, why that lets it catch broken views long before they reach production, and how it is set to become part of Rails 8.2. They also get into how ReActionView makes Rails views reactive without rewriting them, the story behind RubyEvents.org, and why tooling like Herb matters even more when AI agents are writing your templates. Listen to this episode (90m) or subscribe to On Rails in your podcast player.
entries.title: On Rails — Marco Roth: Teaching Rails to Read Its Own Template

entries.summary: Hi, Wojtek here. Let’s explore this week’s changes with another big round of fixes in the Rails codebase.
entries.text: Hi, Wojtek here. Let’s explore this week’s changes with another big round of fixes in the Rails codebase. Add a guide for using Hotwire with Rails The guide can already be read on the Edge Guides. Use an Array for storing Active Record attributes Cast and freeze a model’s attribute defaults when its schema is loaded. Deprecate unscope(where: :column) removing conditions on other tables An unqualified column passed to unscope(where: ...) currently removes conditions on every table that has a column of that name, including joined and eager loaded tables. In Rails 9.0 it will only remove conditions on the relation’s own table. Detect Kamal in app:update command The update command didn’t pass skip_kamal, so it rendered config files as if every application deployed with Kamal. Filter parameters from the message logged when a command can’t be handled When a channel action raised, the error log included the raw WebSocket message, so values hidden by filter_parameters in the action’s debug log were written in clear at the error level. Cast numeric values to the scale of the PostgreSQL money type money only rounded strings to its scale, so a numeric value was held unrounded and as given, while it was rounded on save and read back as a BigDecimal. Qualify unscope values with table name when merging relations Fixes an issue where merging a relation with an unscope(where: ...) clause unscoped conditions on joined or eager loaded tables that share the same column name. entries.summary: Hi, it’s Greg, bringing you the latest changes in the Rails codebase. It was a busy week, with a lot of changes, so buckle up!
entries.text: Hi, it’s Greg, bringing you the latest changes in the Rails codebase. It was a busy week, with a lot of changes, so buckle up! Rails 8.0.5.2 and 8.1.4.1 have been released! These are security releases, addressing 21 security issues, so you should upgrade if you haven’t already. Allow anonymous subclasses of cache stores with LocalCache A recent change built the local cache’s registry key from the store’s class name in initialize, and that name is nil for an anonymous class, so Class.new(ActiveSupport::Cache::MemoryStore).new blew up with a NoMethodError. Anonymous stores are handy in tests to record what a request writes to the cache, and they work again. Fix Active Record includes with merge of an order on another model Merging a relation that orders by another model’s table lost the reference to that table, so includes didn’t know it had to join it. The merge now records the references for the order values it copies over. Accept bind values in where! and having! again where! and having! are :nodoc:, but plenty of apps and gems call them with bind values, Discourse and Canvas among them. A recent refactor made where!("id = ?", 1) raise a NoMethodError, and this brings the old signature back. Skip nested values that serialize to an empty query in to_query { q: [[]], page: 2 }.to_query returned "&page=2" with a stray separator in front, and since url_for passes extra options through, you ended up with URLs like /search?&page=2. entries.text: Hello, Rails community! Rails Versions 8.0.5.2 and 8.1.4.1 have been released. These are security updates addressing 21 security issues falling into a few themes: Possible arbitrary file read, file write and remote code execution in Active Storage image and video processing Possible Strong Parameters bypass in Parameters#each_key Possible IP spoofing in remote_ip through the Forwarded header (8.1 only) Multiple possible XSS vulnerabilities in Action View helpers, and one in the Active Support MessagePack serializer (8.1 only) Possible DoS vulnerabilities in Active Support safe_constantize, Action Controller Live streaming, and Active Storage proxy mode and filename handling Unsigned Content-Type and unenforced file size in Active Storage direct uploads to Google Cloud Storage Session handling issues: a destroyed session restored by CacheStore, a session cookie leaked by Active Storage proxy mode, and a missing SameSite attribute on session cookies Possible cache poisoning through content negotiation Possible signature replay in Action Mailbox Mailgun ingress We strongly recommend upgrading as soon as possible. Older versions of Rails are unsupported, and users are recommended to upgrade to at least the 8.0 series. Security support for the 8.0 series ends on November 7, 2026. See our maintenance policy for details. entries.summary: Hi, it’s Claudio Baccigalupo. Don’t be scared 🎃 this week’s changes to the Rails codebase are all treats. Let’s explore them.
entries.text: Hi, it’s Claudio Baccigalupo. Don’t be scared 🎃 this week’s changes to the Rails codebase are all treats. Let’s explore them. New guide to multiple databases in Active Record As part of the Rails Foundation effort, the refreshed guide is live, tackling the three-tier production configuration that new apps get by default. Tuning performance for deployment guide open for review A PR that updates the guide to performance tuning is open. Your feedback is helpful, especially if you have experience tuning Rails apps in production. Don’t load Capybara and Selenium on boot in new applications The generated Gemfile now declares capybara and selenium-webdriver with require: false. ActionDispatch::SystemTestCase already requires both when a system test is loaded, so test processes that don’t run system tests boot faster. Don’t render authenticity tokens under the :header_only CSRF strategy :header_only verifies requests by their Sec-Fetch-Site header and never reads a token, yet forms, button_to and csrf_meta_tags were still generating one on every render. Now they render none, so a page’s bytes no longer change from one request to the next. Process each Action Cable connection’s commands in order Commands from the same connection could previously run at the same time or out of order. entries.title: No tricks, just treats

entries.summary: New apps stop falling back to Marshal for signed messages, the local secret file is no longer world-readable, and SQLite finally renames columns the way the database intended.
entries.text: New apps stop falling back to Marshal for signed messages, the local secret file is no longer world-readable, and SQLite finally renames columns the way the database intended. Here’s what’s new in Rails: Default config.active_support.message_serializer to :json for 8.2 With config.load_defaults 8.2, messages from MessageVerifier and MessageEncryptor no longer fall back to deserializing Marshal payloads. That covers signed IDs, signed GlobalIDs, Active Storage keys, and the rest. Apps on 7.1 through 8.1 keep :json_allow_marshal. Confirm nothing still arrives as Marshal via the message_serializer_fallback.active_support notification before you switch. Create tmp/local_secret.txt with owner-only permissions The development and test secret_key_base file was created with the process umask, often 022, so it was world-readable. It is now written as 0600, and an existing file is tightened on read on non-Windows platforms, matching config/master.key. Keep route redirects from a string template on the request host redirect("/%{path}") could turn GET /old/%2Finjected.example into //injected.example, which browsers follow to another host. When interpolation would give the target a scheme or host the template does not name, the delimiter is now percent-encoded. Templates that already name a host, such as redirect("//cdn.example.com/%{path}"), are unchanged. entries.summary: Hussain Akram is an engineering manager at Donorbox and Antonio Carlos de Souza (A.C.) is its chief architect, working on a Rails app that has helped nonprofits raise money online and in person for more than a decade.
entries.text: Hussain Akram is an engineering manager at Donorbox and Antonio Carlos de Souza (A.C.) is its chief architect, working on a Rails app that has helped nonprofits raise money online and in person for more than a decade. Robby, Hussain, and A.C. get into how Donorbox handles serious traffic with a deliberately boring setup, why the team moved CI back onto developers' machines, and how they're pulling older parts of the app back toward Rails defaults. They also talk about how they use agent docs to steer AI tools toward the patterns they want the codebase to follow. Links: Donorbox Solid Queue Herb Fizzy Lexxy RuboCop Rails Omakase Brakeman Agile Web Development with Rails Eloquent Ruby by Russ Olsen Practical Object-Oriented Design in Ruby by Sandi Metz The Pragmatic Programmer by Andrew Hunt and David Thomas Listen to this episode on Buzzsprout (1h 47m) or subscribe to On Rails in your podcast player of choice.
entries.title: On Rails — Hussain Akram & Antonio Carlos de Souza: Rails Scales for the Rest of Us

entries.summary: Hi, it’s Vipul. Let’s explore this week’s changes in the Rails codebase.
entries.text: Hi, it’s Vipul. Let’s explore this week’s changes in the Rails codebase. Agents on Rails: Can a model build on its own work? Stage 3 adds multi-step tasks where each ticket starts a fresh session, while files and notes carry forward. The benchmark now combines all three stages into one leaderboard, with tasks spanning legacy applications and new projects. Here are some highlights from the changes merged to Rails main this week. Speed up String#blank? for ASCII strings String#blank? now checks ASCII-only strings by scanning their bytes instead of running a regular expression. Strings containing non-ASCII characters keep the existing regexp path and its encoding-specific whitespace handling. A follow-up removes repeated bytesize calls from the scan. Share read-only default attributes in Active Record Active Record now shares a read-only set of default attributes when it can, with a per-Ractor fallback for defaults that cannot be shared. In the PR author’s ruby-bench Active Record run, average time excluding warm-up iterations fell from 199 ms to 170 ms; the same PR reports 134 ms for Rails 8.1.4. Render collections with fewer intermediate objects Action View now renders collection partials into one shared output buffer when neither collection caching nor a per-item layout needs the items separately. entries.summary: Now that we understand better how agents deal with contained tasks and contained codebases, it’s time to push them a little harder.
entries.text: Now that we understand better how agents deal with contained tasks and contained codebases, it’s time to push them a little harder. Stage 3 adds a set of large multi-step tasks that test how well a model can build on its own work over multiple sessions without turning it into a hot mess. We’ve also greatly expanded the variety of apps we test the models on. Finally, we revisited Stages 1 and 2 to combine all three into a single benchmark that answers one question: which model is the best all-rounder for tasks large and small in your Rails apps? We chose nine models for this stage and used our test runs to pick reasoning settings, aiming to balance capability and cost. We ran Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol at xhigh; Grok 4.7 at high; and GPT-6 Luna, Kimi K3, DeepSeek 4.1 Flash, GLM 5.3 Flash and Muse Spark 1.3 at max. We also tested Opus and Astra at medium to see what extra effort buys. Here are the results: And these are the highlights: Most accurate: Claude Opus 5.5 at xhigh, with 65.3% success. It also leads on the new multi-step tasks in Stage 3, at 72.2%. Cheapest: GPT-6 Luna at max, with 43.4% success for about $0.19 per run. Fastest: GPT-6 Astra at medium, 16m 36s mean time per run with 62.3% success. Best combination of all three: GPT-6.1 Sol at xhigh: 60.8% credit, about $0.80 and 23m 35s per run. Why Stage 3? Stage 1 asked whether a model knows Rails. Stage 2 asked whether it can ship a feature. Both give the agent one session and a prepared codebase.
entries.title: Agents on Rails: Stage 3. Can a model build on its own work?
